Lift
LIFT
v.
Old Norse lypta, “to raise.” Renders the Hebrew nāsā’, “to lift, carry, bear,” and rūm, “to be high, exalted”; and the Greek epairō, “to lift up,” hupsoō, “to exalt,” and airo, “to take up, lift.”

Biblical Definition

Lift in Scripture is the verb of upward motion in worship, intercession, blessing, and divine help. The saint lifts up his hands in prayer (let us lift up our heart with our hands unto God in the heavens); he lifts up his voice in praise and supplication; he lifts up his eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh his help; he lifts up the head of the bowed-down in Christ-shaped consolation; he lifts up holy hands without wrath and doubting; he lifts the fallen to their feet. God lifts: He is the lifter up of mine head; He lifteth up the meek; He lifteth up the poor out of the dust, and the needy from the dunghill; He lifts up His countenance upon His people in the Aaronic blessing. Christ lifts: He lifted up His eyes to the Father at Lazarus’s tomb and in the high-priestly prayer; He lifted up His hands and blessed the disciples as He was parted from them and carried up into heaven. And, supremely, Christ Himself is lifted up—on the cross (as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up), at His resurrection, at His ascension, and at the Father’s right hand. The verb’s grammar is therefore the gospel grammar: the lifted Christ lifts His people from death to life, from the dust to the heavenly places, from the bowed-down posture of guilt to the upright posture of sons. To lift up the hands, the voice, the eyes, the head, and the heart is the embodied liturgy of the saved—the bodily echo of the inward exaltation of the soul that has been lifted by grace and now lives in the upward motion that grace produces.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LIFT as to raise; to elevate; to bear or carry upward; figuratively, to raise to dignity, honor, or office; to exalt.

expand to see more

LIFT, v.t. — 1. To raise; to elevate; as, to lift the hand, the head, the foot. 2. To raise from anything depressing; as, to lift up the head, the heart. 3. To raise in dignity, condition, or rank; to elevate; as, to lift to office. 4. In scripture, to elate; to make haughty; as, his heart was lifted up.

LIFTING, ppr. — Raising; bearing up; elevating; exalting.

Key Scripture

Psalm 121:1-2 — "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth."

1 Timothy 2:8 — "I will therefore that men pray every where, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting."

John 3:14 — "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up."

Luke 24:50-51 — "And he led them out as far as to Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven."

Modern Corruption

The biblical lifting of hands, eyes, voice, and head is corrupted by the embarrassment of the rationalist evangelical register that has stiffened the body in worship into hands-in-pockets passivity—and by the inverse extreme of stage-managed performance lifting in charismatic spectacle that empties the gesture of its biblical content.

expand to see more

Much of the rationalist evangelical register has stiffened the body in worship into a posture of hands-in-pockets passivity that the Bible does not know. Scripture is unabashed about the body in worship: lifted hands (Ps 28:2; 63:4; 134:2; 1 Tim 2:8), lifted eyes (Ps 121:1; 123:1; Luke 24:50), lifted voice (Acts 4:24), bowed heads and bent knees in confession, prostrate bodies in awe—the soul’s adoration finding embodied expression because man is body-and-soul together and worships as he is. The cultural memory of revivalist emotionalism has produced, in much of the Reformed and quietly evangelical world, an over-correction in which any bodily lifting is read as suspicious enthusiasm and the believer is implicitly instructed to keep his hands at his sides. The text is sharper than this. I will therefore that men pray every where, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting is not an optional posture for the temperamentally exuberant; it is the apostolic instruction for the body in prayer.

The opposite corruption is the stage-managed performance lifting of certain charismatic spectacle, in which the gesture has become disconnected from its biblical content and functions chiefly as a marker of in-group emotional intensity. The hands go up because the music swells, not because the soul has been moved to adore; the bodily form has become its own reference. Recover the biblical content, and the lifting recovers its meaning. The hands go up because the heart has gone up; the eyes go up because the help comes from above; the voice goes up because the soul has been given something to declare; the head goes up because the Father has lifted what guilt and sorrow had bowed. Both the over-stiffened and the over-performed traditions can find their cure in the same place: in recovering the Bible’s own grammar of lifting, which is the embodied liturgy of a people whose Lord has been lifted up, and who live forever after in the upward motion that grace produces.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nāsā’ (to lift, carry, bear) and rūm (to be high); Greek epairō (to lift up), hupsoō (to exalt), and airo (to take up)—the upward verb of worship, intercession, blessing, and the lifted Christ.

expand to see more

Hebrew nāsā’ (H5375) — to lift, carry, bear (the great verb behind “lift up” in the Psalms).

Hebrew rūm (H7311) — to be high, exalted, lifted up.

Greek epairō (G1869) — to lift up (eyes, hands, voice, the head).

Greek hupsoō (G5312) — to exalt, lift up (used of Christ’s being lifted up on the cross in John 3:14; 12:32).

Usage

"The lifted Christ lifts His people; the embodied liturgy of lifted hands, eyes, voice, and head is the bodily echo of the inward exaltation grace produces."

"Hands-in-pockets passivity is not biblical reverence; it is the cultural over-correction of a tradition that has forgotten the apostolic instruction to lift holy hands."

"As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up—all the lesser liftings in Scripture echo the supreme lifting at the cross."
